extracted.intended_audience: lay students and readers of philosophy of science; undergraduate students of science/philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for defining and evaluating scientific knowledge, scientific method, and natural law — their limits, origin, and relation to human perception and mental constructs. Useful for deciding what counts as a scientific fact, law, or meaningful knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individuality of objects (sameness of sense-impressions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The individuality of an object consists for us in the sameness of the great majority of our sense-impressions at two instants of time; in practice the test of identity is sameness in sense-impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When impressions differ only slightly (e.g. leaves moved by wind), we term them the same individual. For rapidly changing groups of impressions, instants must be taken closer together. Do not postulate a hidden "thing-in-itself" to account for permanence when sameness of impressions suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject postulating 'things-in-themselves' as explanatory
rubrics_metrics.description: Postulating a shadowy 'thing-in-itself' behind sense-impressions (whether called Matter, God, Will, or Mind-stuff) lies beyond the field of conception based on sense-impressions and does not assist in explaining why groups of impressions remain linked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such unknowables are fantasy, not fact; avoid introducing metaphysical entities outside the sphere of sense-impressions when explaining permanency or identity. Work where empirical harvest can be garnered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific facts are constructs based on sense-impressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Immediate sense-impressions form permanent impresses in the brain; their union with associated stored impressions leads to the formation of 'constructs' which we project 'outside ourselves' and term phenomena. The real world for us lies in such constructs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Science's field is essentially the contents of the mind (these constructs). Scientific inquiry and method apply to these constructs and the relations we infer among them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consciousness definition and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: When an interval elapses between sense-impression and exertion filled by cerebral activity marking revival and combination of past sense-impressions, we are said to think or to be conscious. Other-consciousness is an inference (an 'eject') not verified by immediate sense-impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consciousness has no meaning beyond nervous systems akin to our own; it is illogical to assert that consciousness or will can exist outside matter or in systems not similar to human nervous systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge meaningless when applied beyond thinkable things
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'knowledge' is meaningless when extended beyond the sphere in which we may legitimately infer consciousness, i.e., to metaphysical terms that do not ultimately flow from sense-impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: We can only meaningfully speak of knowledge within the plane of human thought; claims about 'things outside thought' are either confused misuse of the term or unanswerable assertions (an 'unmeaning x among an unthinkable y and z').

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific method: classification, comparison, and brief formula discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: The scientific method consists in careful and often laborious classification of facts, in the comparison of their relationships and sequences, and finally in the discovery (by disciplined imagination) of a brief statement or formula which in a few words resumes a wide range of facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification denotes systematic association of kindred facts — the collection of relevant and crucial facts, not mere accumulation. The goal is economy of thought and enabling fitting exertion on receipt of a novel group of impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of scientific law
rubrics_metrics.description: A scientific law (or 'natural law') is a brief statement or formula which resumes the relationship between a group of facts; a formula that, by mental shorthand, replaces a lengthy description of sequences among sense-impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the notion of 'formula' to avoid confusion with juridical law. A scientific law is a mental resume: it exists as such only when formulated by human minds and involves mental conceptions outside the immediate field of the phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific law is a product of human mind (man as maker)
rubrics_metrics.description: A scientific law is essentially a product of the human mind and has no meaning apart from man; it owes its existence to the creative power of intellect — e.g., Newton associated the idea of mutual acceleration with observed sequences to create the law of gravitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law does not pre-exist independently in an unconditioned universe; the formation of concepts, classification, and generalization are required before a law exists. It is more accurate to say 'man gives laws to Nature' than the converse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural law is relative to perceptive faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'outside world' (and thus natural law) is a construct conditioned by the perceptive and retentive faculties of man. Natural law has no relation to 'things-in-themselves' apart from man's mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Universal validity of natural law is meaningful only with respect to a certain type of perceptive faculty (normal human beings). Thought experiments (Clerk-Maxwell's demon) illustrate that beings with different perceptive powers might not regard the same sequences as 'laws'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal validity of scientific law limited by stability of perceptive faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: A scientific law is valid for all normal human beings and is unchangeable so long as their perceptive faculties remain without material modification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'universal' validity is relative: if perceptive faculties change (e.g., across species, cultures, or evolutionary stages), the applicability or meaning of a law may change. Be cautious in asserting absolute universality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish juridical/legal law from scientific law
rubrics_metrics.description: Juridical law (Austin's definition) is a rule laid down by an intelligent being for guidance of another, implying command and duty; scientific law is descriptive, not prescriptive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate the two senses of 'law' — misuse leads to 'muddy speculation'. When discussing 'law' be explicit about whether the juridical or scientific sense is intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequences of perceptions are not laws until formulated
rubrics_metrics.description: A repeated sequence of perceptions (e.g., planets moving) is not in itself a law. The sequence must be compared with other sequences, classified, generalized, and mental conceptions formed before a concise and comprehensive formula worthy of the name 'scientific law' exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely observing and describing phenomena, however full, does not constitute a law. The creation of mental shorthand (concepts) that summarizes and relates phenomena is essential to define a law.
